Practical guides to help you write a resume that gets interviews, answer interview questions with confidence, and keep growing once you are hired — explained in plain English, with real examples you can copy and adapt.

Whether you are applying for your first job, changing careers in your thirties or forties, or preparing to ask for the promotion you have earned, you will find a step-by-step guide here that walks you through exactly what to say, what to write, and what to avoid.

Start Here

Finding a job is a skill — and skills can be learned

Most people are never taught how hiring actually works. They send the same resume to forty job adverts, hear nothing back, and assume the problem is their experience. In reality, the problem is usually presentation. Recruiters spend only a few seconds on a first scan of each application, applicant tracking software filters resumes before a human ever sees them, and interviewers decide far more on how clearly you explain your value than on the length of your job history.

That is good news, because presentation can be fixed in a weekend. A resume rewritten around achievements instead of duties, a cover letter that speaks directly to one employer instead of every employer, and interview answers prepared with a simple structure will outperform a longer career history presented badly. Every guide on Career Boost is built around that idea: small, concrete improvements that compound into interviews, offers, and promotions.

If you are starting from zero, begin with our guide on how to find a job with no experience, which shows where entry-level opportunities actually hide and how to make volunteering, coursework, and personal projects count. If you are still studying or freshly graduated, how to write a CV with no experience will help you fill a professional-looking document even when your work history is short.

Resume Writing

A resume that gets interviews, not just applause

Your resume has one job: to make a busy recruiter think, within seconds, "this person can do our job." Everything on the page either supports that thought or gets in its way. The strongest resumes lead with a short professional summary, describe each role with measurable achievements, and mirror the language of the job advert so both software and humans can see the match. Our complete walkthrough, how to write a resume that gets interviews, takes you section by section through the format recruiters prefer, with before-and-after bullet points you can adapt to your own roles.

A resume rarely travels alone. Most employers still read cover letters, and a good one can rescue an average resume by explaining the story behind it — why you are changing direction, why this company, why now. Learn how to write a cover letter that stands out without sounding like everyone else, and if your history includes time away from work, read how to explain a gap in your CV so you can address it calmly and briefly instead of hoping nobody notices.

Your online presence matters just as much as the document you send. Recruiters routinely search for candidates after reading a resume, which is why our LinkedIn profile tips show you how to write a headline and summary that make you look like the obvious person to message.

Interview Preparation

Walk into the interview already knowing the questions

Interviews feel unpredictable, but they are not. The same core questions appear in almost every hiring process, because employers are all trying to answer the same three things: can you do the work, will you fit the team, and will you stay? Our most-read guide, 20 common interview questions and how to answer them, gives you a model answer structure for each one, and the companion piece on how to answer "tell me about yourself" helps you open the conversation with a two-minute summary that sets the tone for everything after it.

How you present yourself matters too. Our guide to what to wear to a job interview explains how to judge the right level of formality for any industry, and if your interview is on a screen rather than in a room, how to prepare for a video interview covers the camera, lighting, technology checks, and etiquette that remote hiring demands.

The interview does not end when you leave the room. A short, well-timed thank-you message can keep you at the front of the hiring manager's mind, and knowing how to follow up after an interview — including what to do when you hear nothing — can be the difference between an offer and silence.

Growing at Work

Getting hired is only the first half of a career

Once you are in a role, a different set of skills decides how far you go. The colleagues who advance fastest are rarely just the most technically capable; they are the ones who communicate clearly, write emails that get answers, handle difficult relationships without drama, and make their contributions visible. Start with how to improve your communication skills at work and how to write a professional email at work — two skills you will use every single day. If your manager is part of the problem rather than the solution, how to handle a difficult boss professionally offers calm, practical strategies that protect both your work and your reputation.

Visibility matters as well. Building a personal brand at work is not about self-promotion for its own sake; it is about making sure the right people know what you are good at, so opportunities come to you instead of passing to whoever happens to be loudest.

Pay and Progression

Ask for what you are worth — and get it in writing

The most expensive mistake in most careers is never negotiating. A slightly higher starting salary compounds through every future raise and every future job that is benchmarked against it. Yet many people accept the first number they are given because nobody taught them how the conversation works. Our guide on how to negotiate your salary with confidence explains how to research your market value, when to raise the subject, and the exact phrases that keep the discussion friendly and firm.

Negotiation does not stop at the offer letter. If you have been performing well in your current role, how to ask for a raise by email gives you word-for-word templates, and when you are ready for the next level entirely, how to ask for a promotion the right way shows you how to build your case months before you ever sit down with your manager. And if the time comes to move on, do it gracefully: how to write a resignation letter includes examples that leave every door open behind you.

Thinking bigger? A change of direction is more common — and more achievable — than most people believe. Read how to switch careers at 30 or 40 for a realistic plan that uses the experience you already have instead of starting over.

Quick Answers

Questions readers ask us most

How long should my resume be?

One page if you have under ten years of experience, two pages if your experience genuinely needs the space. Recruiters scan quickly, so every line must earn its place. Our resume guide shows what to cut first.

Can I get a job with no experience at all?

Yes — employers hire beginners every day. The key is presenting transferable evidence: coursework, volunteering, personal projects, and part-time work all count when you describe them as achievements. See how to find a job with no experience.

When is the right time to talk about salary?

Ideally after the employer wants you — once you have an offer, your negotiating position is strongest. Research your range early, but let them name the first number where possible. The full method is in our salary negotiation guide.

Is it too late to change careers at 40?

No. Career changers in their thirties and forties bring transferable skills, professional maturity, and networks that younger applicants do not have. The trick is translating that experience into the new field's language — see how to switch careers at 30 or 40.

More answers on our full FAQ page.

How to Write a Resume That Gets Interviews

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 12 min read

A good resume does not list everything you have ever done. It proves, quickly and clearly, that you can do the job being advertised. Recruiters typically spend six to ten seconds on their first scan of a resume, and before a human even sees it, an applicant tracking system (ATS) may already have filtered it against the keywords in the job advert. Writing a resume that gets interviews means satisfying both audiences: software that looks for matching skills, and a busy person who needs to spot your value at a glance. This guide walks you through every section, in the order employers expect, with examples you can adapt today.

Step 1: Choose the right format

For most people, the reverse-chronological format works best: your most recent job first, then earlier roles in descending order. Recruiters prefer it because it shows your career story at a glance, and ATS software parses it reliably. Use a functional or skills-only format only if you are changing careers or have a long gap — and even then, a hybrid format (a skills summary followed by a brief chronological history) usually performs better. Keep the design simple: one clean font, clear headings, no tables, text boxes, photos, or graphics. Fancy templates are the most common reason good candidates get filtered out by software before a person ever sees their name.

Length matters too. One page is right for students, graduates, and anyone with under ten years of experience. Two pages are acceptable for experienced professionals, but only if every line earns its place. Three pages is almost always too long.

Step 2: Write a header that makes contact effortless

Your header needs five things: your full name, your professional title or target role, your city and country, a professional email address, and your phone number. Add a link to your LinkedIn profile if it is complete and current — our LinkedIn profile tips show how to bring it up to standard. Skip your full home address, date of birth, and marital status; modern employers neither need nor expect them, and they waste the most valuable line on the page.

Step 3: Open with a professional summary, not an objective

The old-style objective ("seeking a challenging position where I can grow") tells the employer what you want. A professional summary tells them what they get. Write three or four lines covering your years of experience, your strongest skills, and one measurable achievement. For example:

Customer service specialist with five years of experience in retail and call-centre environments. Consistently rated in the top 10% of the team for customer satisfaction, with a record of resolving 95% of issues on first contact. Skilled in complaint handling, team training, and CRM software.

Notice that every claim is specific and most are measurable. Rewrite this summary for every application, mirroring the priorities in the job advert.

Step 4: Turn duties into achievements in your experience section

This is where most resumes fail. Listing duties ("responsible for handling invoices") says what the job was. Listing achievements says how well you did it. Use this formula for every bullet point: strong action verb + what you did + measurable result. Compare the difference:

  • Weak: "Responsible for social media accounts."
  • Strong: "Grew the company Instagram account from 2,000 to 11,500 followers in eight months by posting daily short-form video content."
  • Weak: "Helped customers with problems."
  • Strong: "Resolved an average of 40 customer queries per day, maintaining a 98% satisfaction rating across 1,200+ reviews."
  • Weak: "In charge of stock and ordering."
  • Strong: "Cut stock waste by 18% in one quarter by introducing a weekly inventory check and renegotiating supplier delivery schedules."

Numbers do not have to be dramatic. Percentages, money saved, time reduced, customers served, projects delivered, and team sizes all count. If you genuinely cannot quantify something, describe its scale or outcome instead: "trained new starters" becomes "trained and mentored six new starters, all of whom passed probation." Aim for three to five bullets per role, ordered with the most impressive first, and give recent roles more space than older ones.

Step 5: Build a skills section the software can find

Read the job advert and list the skills it names — tools, software, certifications, and methods. Then include every one you genuinely have, using the same wording the advert uses. If the advert says "Microsoft Excel," write "Microsoft Excel," not "spreadsheets." Present skills as a simple comma-separated list or short lines, and group them if you have many (for example: Technical, Languages, Certifications). Never claim a skill you cannot demonstrate in an interview; the lie always surfaces, usually at the worst moment.

Step 6: Education, and what to do if you are short on experience

List your highest qualifications first, with the institution and year. If you graduated within the last three years, you can add relevant modules, your dissertation topic, or academic achievements. Experienced professionals should keep this section brief — your work history now speaks louder. If your paid experience is thin, do not panic and do not pad. Move relevant projects, volunteering, internships, and freelance work into the experience section and describe them with the same achievement formula. Our dedicated guide on how to write a CV with no experience covers this situation in full.

Step 7: Tailor the resume to every single job

Sending one generic resume to forty adverts produces forty silences. Tailoring takes fifteen minutes: adjust your summary to match the role, reorder your bullets so the most relevant achievements come first, and make sure the skills section mirrors the advert's language. Keep a master document with everything you have ever done, then copy and trim it for each application. Employers can feel the difference instantly — a tailored resume reads like an answer to their advert, because it is one.

Mistakes that quietly cost you interviews

  • Spelling and grammar errors. The single fastest way to be rejected. Read the final version aloud and have someone else check it.
  • An unprofessional email address. Create a simple firstname.lastname address for job hunting.
  • Personal pronouns and paragraphs. Resumes use fragments, not "I was responsible for…" sentences.
  • Lying about dates, titles, or skills. Background checks and probation periods expose exaggeration.
  • Sending the wrong file format. PDF unless the advert asks otherwise, named clearly: Firstname-Lastname-Resume.pdf.
  • Including references or "references available on request." Both waste space; employers will ask when they want them.

Your final checklist

Before you send: Is the format clean and ATS-friendly? Does the summary match this specific job? Does every bullet start with an action verb, and do most include a result? Does the skills section mirror the advert? Is it one or two pages, error-free, and saved as a clearly named PDF? If yes, send it — and then strengthen the package with a tailored cover letter that stands out. A resume built this way will not get you every interview, but it will get you the interviews your experience deserves.

20 Common Interview Questions and How to Answer Them

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 16 min read

Interviewers are not trying to trick you. Behind nearly every question sits one of three concerns: can this person do the job, will they work well with our team, and are they likely to stay and grow? Once you understand what each question is really testing, you can prepare honest, structured answers in advance — and preparation is the real difference between candidates who sound confident and candidates who hope for the best.

For experience-based questions, use the STAR method: describe the Situation, the Task you faced, the Action you took, and the Result. Keep each answer between one and two minutes. Here are the twenty questions you are most likely to face, what they test, and how to answer each one well.

1. "Tell me about yourself."

This is an invitation to summarise your professional story, not your life story. Use the present–past–future structure covered fully in our guide on how to answer "tell me about yourself": where you are now, the experience that got you here, and why this role is the logical next step.

2. "Why do you want this job?"

They are testing motivation and research. Connect two or three specific things about the role or company — its products, customers, growth, or values — to your own skills and goals. Generic answers ("it's a great company") convince nobody.

3. "Why should we hire you?"

Summarise your match against the advert: the key skills you bring, one standout achievement, and what you understand about their needs. This is your closing argument; make it specific, not modest.

4. "What is your greatest strength?"

Choose a strength the job actually needs and prove it with a short example. "I'm organised" is a claim; "I managed the schedules of a twelve-person team without a missed deadline last year" is evidence.

5. "What is your greatest weakness?"

Pick a real but manageable weakness and, most importantly, what you are doing about it. "I used to struggle with delegating, so I now assign tasks with clear checkpoints — my last project finished a week early" shows self-awareness and growth. Avoid clichés like "I'm a perfectionist" with no substance behind them.

6. "Tell me about a challenge you faced at work."

A pure STAR question. Choose a genuine difficulty, spend most of your answer on your actions, and end with a positive, measurable result. Never blame colleagues or managers for the problem.

7. "Where do you see yourself in five years?"

They want ambition that fits their organisation. Describe growth that this role naturally leads to — deeper expertise, more responsibility, mentoring others — rather than a plan that requires leaving in a year.

8. "Why are you leaving your current job?"

Stay positive and forward-looking: growth, new challenges, a better fit. Never criticise your current employer, however justified it feels. Negativity makes interviewers wonder what you will say about them one day.

9. "Tell me about a time you worked in a team."

Show collaboration, not just attendance. Describe your role, how you handled a disagreement or a struggling teammate, and the shared result. Teams succeed or fail on behaviour, and that is what they are listening for.

10. "How do you handle pressure or tight deadlines?"

Describe your actual system: prioritising, breaking work into steps, communicating early when timelines slip. Then give one brief example where the system worked under real pressure.

11. "What is your greatest professional achievement?"

Choose the achievement closest to this job's needs, quantify it, and explain why it mattered to the business — revenue, savings, quality, customers. Pride is welcome here; exaggeration is not.

12. "Tell me about a mistake you made."

Own a real mistake, explain what you learned, and describe the safeguard you built afterwards. Interviewers are testing honesty and growth, and everyone has a genuine example. "I have never made one" ends the conversation about your credibility.

13. "How do you prioritise your work?"

Explain a method: urgency versus importance, deadlines, impact on others. Mention tools you use and how you renegotiate when everything arrives at once. A concrete system beats "I just stay organised."

14. "Why is there a gap in your employment?"

Be brief, honest, and unembarrassed: state the reason, mention anything productive from the period, and pivot to your readiness now. Our guide on how to explain a gap in your CV gives exact wording for the common situations.

15. "What do you know about our company?"

Research before the interview: what the company sells, who its customers are, recent news, and its main competitors. Two or three informed sentences separate you from most of the field.

16. "How do you handle feedback or criticism?"

Give an example where feedback stung, you applied it, and your work improved. Employers want coachable people; defensiveness in the answer predicts defensiveness in the job.

17. "Describe a difficult decision you had to make."

Show reasoning under uncertainty: the options, the criteria you used, the outcome, and what you would refine next time. Judgement, not luck, is the point.

18. "What are your salary expectations?"

Research the market range first and answer with a range anchored in that research, expressing flexibility and interest in the whole package. Our salary negotiation guide explains the strategy in depth; if you can politely delay until an offer arrives, do.

19. "Are you applying to other companies?"

Honesty with discretion: it is fine to say you are speaking with a few organisations but that this role is your first choice, and why. Never invent competing offers to create pressure.

20. "Do you have any questions for us?"

Always ask. Good options: "What does success look like in this role in the first six months?", "What is the team structure?", "What are the next steps in the process?" Asking nothing signals low interest, whatever you said earlier. And after the interview, keep the momentum with a proper follow-up and thank-you email.

How to practise without sounding rehearsed

Write bullet points for each answer, not scripts. Memorised scripts collapse under follow-up questions; bullet points let you adapt while keeping your structure. Practise aloud — answers always sound different spoken — and record yourself once to catch rambling. Prepare two or three strong STAR stories in advance, because a single good story about a challenge, a team success, and a mistake will cover half the questions on this list. Preparation is not about performing a character; it is about removing panic so the real you can be heard.

How to Write a Cover Letter That Stands Out

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 11 min read

Many applicants treat the cover letter as an afterthought, or skip it entirely when the application form marks it "optional." That is a missed opportunity. Your resume lists what you have done; the cover letter explains why it matters to this employer, in this role, right now. It is also the only part of your application written in your own voice, which makes it the best tool you have for showing personality, motivation, and genuine interest. A strong cover letter follows a simple four-paragraph structure. Here is how to write each part — and a complete example at the end.

Before you write: research for ten minutes

Standing out starts before the first sentence. Read the job advert closely and note the three requirements the employer emphasises most. Then look at the company's website: what do they sell, who are their customers, what have they announced recently? You are looking for two things — the specific problems this role exists to solve, and one genuine reason you want to work there rather than anywhere else. Ten minutes of research gives your letter the specificity that generic letters never have.

Also find a name if you possibly can. "Dear Ms. Rahman" outperforms "To whom it may concern" every time. Check the advert, the company website, or LinkedIn for the hiring manager or team lead. If no name exists anywhere, "Dear Hiring Team" is an acceptable, friendly fallback.

Paragraph 1: The opening — role, hook, and your strongest claim

State the role you are applying for and lead immediately with your single most relevant credential. Skip throat-clearing like "I am writing to express my interest in…" — everyone writes that. Compare:

Weak: "I am writing to apply for the Marketing Assistant position advertised on your website. I believe I would be a great fit for your team."

Strong: "As a marketing assistant who grew a small retailer's Instagram following from 2,000 to 11,500 in eight months, I was excited to see your opening for a Marketing Assistant — the role's focus on short-form video is exactly where I do my best work."

The strong version proves fit in two lines and gives the reader a reason to continue.

Paragraph 2: The match — your evidence against their needs

This is the body of the letter: two or three achievements matched directly against the advert's main requirements. Do not repeat your resume word for word; select the highlights and add the context the resume has no room for — the size of the team, the difficulty of the situation, the result. Quantify wherever you can. If the advert asks for someone who can "manage multiple projects," do not just claim you can; describe the semester, season, or campaign where you did exactly that.

Paragraph 3: The connection — why this company, why you fit

Now show this letter could not have been sent anywhere else. Mention something specific: a product you use, a campaign you admired, the company's expansion into a market you know, or values that match how you work. Then connect it back to what you offer. This paragraph is where career changers explain their move positively ("After six years in hospitality, I am bringing my customer experience into…") and where applicants with a gap in their CV can address it in one calm sentence rather than leaving the reader to wonder.

Paragraph 4: The close — confident and simple

Thank the reader, restate your enthusiasm briefly, and invite the next step. "I would welcome the chance to discuss how my experience could support your team's goals this year. Thank you for your time and consideration." Sign off with "Sincerely" or "Best regards" and your full name. No begging, no "I await your favourable response," and no listing your phone number five ways — your resume header already has it.

A complete example

Dear Mr. Osei,

As a customer service representative who maintained a 98% satisfaction rating across more than 1,200 customer reviews last year, I was delighted to see your opening for a Customer Support Specialist. Your company's reputation for resolving problems on the first contact matches exactly how I like to work.

In my current role at a busy online retailer, I handle around forty enquiries a day across phone, email, and live chat. Last winter I noticed the same delivery question appearing repeatedly, so I drafted a set of clearer tracking messages that our team adopted — repeat contacts about deliveries fell by a third within a month. I also train new starters on our support software, which has given me a practical understanding of what consistent, well-documented answers do for a whole team's numbers.

I have followed your company's growth into home delivery with real interest, as a customer as well as a professional. Supporting customers through a service that is still expanding — where feedback genuinely shapes how things improve — is the kind of work I find most rewarding, and it is why I am applying to you rather than to a larger, more settled operation.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience could contribute to your support team. Thank you for considering my application.

Best regards,
Amelia Hart

Phrases to delete from your draft

  • "I am a team player with excellent communication skills." Unproven claims. Show the team, the project, the result instead.
  • "To whom it may concern." Find a name, or use "Dear Hiring Team."
  • "I believe I would be perfect for this role." Confidence is good; perfection claims are noise. Evidence persuades, adjectives do not.
  • "Please do not hesitate to contact me." Weak and dated. "I would welcome the chance to discuss…" is stronger.
  • Any sentence copied from a template site unchanged. Recruiters read hundreds of letters; they recognise boilerplate instantly.

Length, format, and final checks

Keep the letter to one page — roughly 250 to 400 words. Use the same font and header style as your resume so the pair look like one document. Save and send as PDF unless told otherwise. Finally, proofread twice: once for errors, and once asking the only question that matters — "does every paragraph say something about me that this specific employer would care about?" If a paragraph could be sent to any company unchanged, rewrite it until it could not.

How to Negotiate Your Salary With Confidence

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 11 min read

Most employers expect you to negotiate. The first salary they offer is rarely the highest they are authorised to pay, and accepting it without a word can cost you far more than one month's difference — because every future raise, bonus percentage, and even your next employer's offer is usually calculated from the number you start with. Yet many people stay silent, afraid that asking will seem greedy or risk the offer. It will not, if you do it the way this guide describes: with research, patience, and a friendly tone throughout.

Step 1: Know your number before anyone asks

Research the market rate for your role, experience level, and location using salary surveys, job adverts for similar roles (many now list ranges), professional associations, and conversations with people in the field. Build three numbers: the market range for the role, your target — a realistic figure near the top of that range — and your walk-away point, below which the job genuinely does not work for you. Factor in the whole picture: commute costs, hours, pension contributions, and benefits all change what a salary is really worth.

Step 2: Delay the salary conversation as long as you can

Your negotiating power grows the more the employer wants you, and it peaks after they have chosen you. If asked about salary expectations early in the process, stay polite and vague: "I'd like to understand the full role and package first — I'm sure we can agree on something fair for the position." If a form forces a number, give your researched range rather than a single figure. When an application or recruiter pushes hard, anchor to the market: "Based on my research for roles like this in this area, I'm seeing a range of X to Y." Never base your ask on your current salary; base it on the value of the job you are moving to.

Step 3: Let them make the first offer — then pause

When the offer comes, thank them warmly and do not accept or react to the number on the spot. Ask for the offer in writing and a day or two to consider it: "Thank you — I'm very excited about the role. Could you send the details in writing so I can review the full package carefully?" This pause is normal, expected, and it gives you time to compare the offer against your research without pressure. If the number matches your target, you may still negotiate modestly or focus on other elements. If it falls short, prepare your counter.

Step 4: Counter with evidence, not feelings

A good counter-offer has three parts: gratitude, evidence, and a specific figure. For example:

"Thank you for the offer — I'm genuinely excited about joining the team. Based on my research into similar roles in this market, and the experience I'll be bringing in [specific skill or achievement], I was expecting a salary closer to [figure]. Is there flexibility to meet me there?"

Notice what this does: it stays enthusiastic, justifies the number with the market and your value, names one clear figure, and ends with an easy question. Ask once, clearly, rather than haggling in small steps. Then stop talking and let them respond — silence after your ask feels uncomfortable, but filling it usually means negotiating against yourself.

Step 5: Negotiate the whole package

Salary is one line of the offer. If the base figure cannot move, other elements often can:

  • A signing bonus or an early salary review after six months, agreed in writing
  • Extra annual leave days
  • Flexible or remote working arrangements
  • Training budgets, certifications, or conference attendance
  • Pension contributions, bonuses, or commission structure
  • Start date, working hours, or job title (which affects your next move)

Sometimes a package with a slightly lower salary but a funded qualification and a six-month review is worth more over two years than the higher figure alone. Run the real numbers before deciding.

Step 6: Get the final agreement in writing

Whatever you agree — salary, review date, bonus terms, flexible arrangements — confirm it by email and make sure the contract reflects it before you sign or resign from your current job. Verbal promises made in a friendly phone call have a way of being remembered differently later. A short, polite email is enough: "Thanks for the conversation — just confirming we've agreed on…" This is not distrust; it is professionalism, and good employers expect it.

What if they say no?

A firm "this is our final offer" is information, not failure. You then decide with clear eyes: does the package, as it stands, beat your current situation and your walk-away point? If yes, accept graciously and enthusiastically — how you accept matters, because these people are about to become your colleagues. If no, decline politely and keep the relationship warm; roles reopen, budgets change, and managers remember gracious candidates. What you should not do is accept an offer you intend to resent, or threaten to walk away unless you genuinely mean it.

The same skills work after you are hired

Negotiation is not a one-time event at the offer stage. The evidence-based approach in this guide — research, timing, a specific figure, a friendly tone — is exactly how you will later ask for a raise by email and build the case to ask for a promotion. Start practising now, with this offer. The worst realistic outcome of a polite, well-researched ask is a no; the likely outcome, over a whole career, is a substantially better-paid one.

LinkedIn Profile Tips: Get Noticed by Recruiters

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 11 min read

Recruiters do not browse LinkedIn hoping to stumble on you. They search it, using keywords for skills, job titles, locations, and tools — and the profiles that appear are the ones that use those words in the right places. A strong LinkedIn profile therefore has two jobs: to be found by search, and then to convince the recruiter within a few seconds that you are worth messaging. This guide rebuilds your profile section by section, in the order recruiters read it.

Your photo and banner: the two-second first impression

Profiles with a photo receive far more views and messages than those without, because recruiters trust and click on real people. Use a recent, well-lit head-and-shoulders photo with a plain background, professional dress appropriate to your industry, and a genuine expression. No sunglasses, group photos, holiday pictures, or heavy filters. Then replace the default blue banner with something simple and relevant — your city skyline, your industry in action, or a clean graphic with your professional tagline. It takes five minutes and instantly separates you from the unfinished profiles.

Your headline: the most valuable line on the page

Your headline appears everywhere — in search results, in comments, in connection requests — yet most people leave it as their current job title alone. Recruiters search for titles and skills, so use the space to combine them. A simple formula works well: Job title | Key skills or specialism | Value you deliver. For example:

  • Basic: "Marketing Assistant at Bright Retail"
  • Strong: "Marketing Assistant | Social Media & Short-Form Video | Grew retail account from 2K to 11.5K followers"
  • Job-seeking graduate: "Business Graduate | Excel, Data Analysis & Reporting | Seeking analyst roles in Manchester"

If you are employed but quietly open to offers, keep your employer's name out of the value section and focus on skills — and check your privacy settings so job-seeking signals are visible to recruiters without being broadcast to your current employer.

The About section: your story in five sentences

Write in the first person, like a professional introduction rather than a legal document. Cover: who you are and your experience level; your strongest skills with a proof point or two; what kind of work energises you; and what you are looking for next, ending with how to reach you. Aim for 150–260 words. The first two lines matter most, because that is all that shows before the "see more" click — put your title, top skills, and best achievement there. Think of this section as your cover letter's permanent cousin: specific, evidenced, and aimed at the reader's needs.

Experience: achievements, not job descriptions

Copying your job description into each role is the most common LinkedIn mistake. Recruiters already know what a sales assistant or an accountant generally does; they want to know what you did. Reuse the strongest bullets from your resume — action verb, task, measurable result — and feel free to add one or two more lines of context than a resume allows. Add media where you can: a presentation, a project link, a photo of work you produced. Rich profiles hold attention longer, and attention is what turns a view into a message.

Skills: choose for search, not for decoration

LinkedIn lets you list many skills, but recruiters filter on a handful of core ones for each role. Pin your top three to match the jobs you want, and make sure the rest of your list uses the standard wording of your industry — the exact terms an advert would use. Then take the skill assessments and gather endorsements from colleagues who have genuinely seen the skill in action. Endorsements from managers and clients carry weight; a wall of endorsements from strangers carries none.

Recommendations: the section most people skip

A short recommendation from a former manager is the closest thing LinkedIn has to a reference letter, and recruiters read them. Ask politely and make it easy: remind the person of the project you worked on together and the qualities you hope they can speak to. Offer to write one for them in return. Two or three specific recommendations beat ten vague ones — "reduced our reporting time by half" persuades; "great team player" does not.

Be visibly active, lightly and consistently

You do not need to become a content creator. Sharing an article with two lines of your own comment, congratulating a former colleague, or posting a short lesson from a project once a week keeps you visible in your network's feed and gives recruiters a sense of a real, engaged professional. Commenting thoughtfully on posts in your field is often more effective than posting yourself, and it takes ten minutes. This steady visibility is also the foundation of building a personal brand at work.

Settings and finishing touches

  • Customise your profile URL to your name (linkedin.com/in/firstname-lastname) and put it on your resume and email signature.
  • Turn on "Open to work" and set it to "recruiters only" if you are currently employed.
  • Complete the Services, Featured, and Licences sections if they apply — certifications are common recruiter filters.
  • Grow your connections deliberately: colleagues, classmates, clients, and people you meet at events. A network of people who actually know you is what produces referrals.
  • Proofread everything. A profile full of typos quietly contradicts every claim of attention to detail.

Set a reminder to update your profile every few months — new skills, new achievements, new goals. A LinkedIn profile is never finished, because your career is not. Keep it current, and it will keep working for you while you sleep.

How to Ask for a Promotion the Right Way

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 11 min read

Many talented people wait silently for their manager to notice their work and offer a promotion. Sometimes that happens. Far more often, the promotion goes to the person who made a clear, well-timed case — not because they were louder, but because they made it easy for their manager to say yes and to defend that yes to the people above them. Asking for a promotion is a professional skill with a learnable method. This guide covers the preparation, the timing, the conversation itself, and what to do with any answer you receive.

First, understand what a promotion actually is

A promotion is not a reward for doing your current job well for a long time. It is the company formally recognising that you are already operating at the next level — or clearly ready to — and that a role at that level exists or can be created. This distinction changes your whole approach. Your case is not "I have worked hard and deserve more." It is "here is the work I am already doing at the higher level, here is its value, and here is the role I propose to grow into." Managers promote evidence, not tenure.

Step 1: Study the next level before you ask for it

Find the job description for the role above yours, or ask your manager directly what distinguishes the two levels in your organisation. Note the gaps between that description and your current work: bigger projects, budget responsibility, mentoring, strategy, client ownership. Then spend the following months deliberately closing the most important gaps and volunteering for work that demonstrates them. If there is no formal description, ask the question that starts every successful promotion case: "What would I need to show over the next six months to be ready for the next level?" Write down the answer — it becomes your checklist and, later, your evidence.

Step 2: Build your evidence file

Memory is a poor negotiator; documentation is an excellent one. Keep a running file — a document, a folder of emails, a note on your phone — recording:

  • Projects you led or delivered, with measurable results: revenue, savings, deadlines beaten, quality improved
  • Positive feedback from clients, senior colleagues, and other departments, saved as it arrives
  • Responsibilities you have absorbed beyond your job description
  • People you have trained, mentored, or covered for
  • Problems you spotted and fixed before they became expensive

Update it monthly, not the night before your review. When the conversation comes, you will speak in specifics while others speak in generalities — and specifics win. The same file powers your raise request and keeps your LinkedIn profile effortlessly current.

Step 3: Choose your moment carefully

Timing can decide the outcome before you say a word. Good moments include your formal performance review, the period just after you have delivered a significant success, and the start of a new budget or planning cycle when headcount and roles are being decided. Poor moments include the middle of a company crisis, the week your manager is dealing with bad results, or the day after a colleague's promotion was announced. If your company promotes on a fixed cycle, work backwards: your case needs to be in your manager's mind before the decision meetings, which usually means raising it three to six months ahead.

Step 4: Run the conversation like a proposal, not a plea

Book a proper meeting rather than ambushing your manager in a corridor. Open by anchoring to the future, then present your evidence, then make the ask:

"I'd like to talk about my path to the senior role. Over the past year I've taken on [evidence: leading the X project, mentoring two new starters, improving Y by 20%]. I believe I'm now consistently working at the level described for the senior position, and I'd like us to agree a plan and a timeline for making that formal. What else would you need to see from me?"

That final question is the most important sentence in the meeting. If your manager cannot promote you today, it converts a flat "no" into a specific, agreed list of targets — and a manager who sets the targets has implicitly committed to honouring them. Get the agreed steps and timeline in a follow-up email, politely: "Thanks for the conversation — confirming the points we agreed…" Then deliver on them visibly.

Handle "not yet" like a professional

A delayed promotion with a clear plan is progress, not rejection. Ask three things: exactly what is missing, how it will be measured, and when you will review it again — then get those dates in the diary. What should concern you is a pattern: vague answers, moving goalposts, or a third consecutive "next cycle" with no specifics. That pattern is information about the organisation, not about your worth, and it may mean your next promotion happens at a different company — at which point your evidence file becomes the backbone of an excellent resume.

Mistakes that quietly kill promotion cases

  • Comparing yourself to colleagues. "She got promoted, so should I" weakens your case. Argue from your own evidence and the role's requirements.
  • Threatening to leave unless you genuinely have an offer and are prepared to go. Ultimatums that are called destroy trust permanently.
  • Asking only about money. A promotion is a role change; discuss scope, title, and development alongside pay, using the approach in our salary negotiation guide.
  • Waiting for the perfect moment that never comes. Preparation matters, but an evidence-backed ask this quarter beats a flawless one imagined for next year.
  • Going quiet after a no. The professionals who eventually get promoted treat the first conversation as the start of a plan, not the end of one.

Asking for a promotion the right way is really a year-long habit: understand the next level, do visible work at that level, document the results, and then present them at the right moment with a clear request. Do that, and you stop hoping to be noticed — you become the easiest promotion decision your manager makes all year.

How to Write a CV With No Experience

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 10 min read

Every experienced professional once had an empty CV, and every employer knows it. Entry-level hiring is not really about experience — it is about evidence of ability, reliability, and willingness to learn. You have more of that evidence than you think: education, projects, volunteering, part-time and family work, sports, and personal projects all demonstrate skills employers pay for. The task is not to invent experience, but to present the experience you already have in a format employers recognise. Here is how, section by section.

Start with the right structure

With little work history, reorder the classic CV. Put your strongest material first: a short personal summary, then education (while it is your strongest asset), then a skills section, then an "Experience" section that honestly includes internships, volunteering, projects, and any paid work — in that order of relevance rather than strict date order. One page is plenty. Use the clean, simple formatting described in our main resume guide: one font, clear headings, no graphics or tables, saved as a PDF.

Write a summary that promises potential, specifically

Your summary is three lines: what you have studied or trained in, your two or three most relevant skills, and the kind of role you are seeking. Avoid empty phrases like "hardworking and motivated" — everyone claims those. Instead, anchor the claim to something concrete:

Recent business graduate with strong Excel and data-entry skills developed through coursework and a six-week internship at a local accountancy firm. Completed a final-year project analysing sales data for a real retail client. Seeking an administrative or junior analyst role where accuracy and organisation matter.

Every phrase there points to proof elsewhere in the document. That is the standard your whole CV should meet.

Make your education work harder

While education is your headline asset, mine it properly. Beyond the institution, qualification, and grades, include: relevant modules (name the ones matching the job), your dissertation or final project and what it involved, academic awards, and any positions of responsibility. If your project involved a real client, real data, fieldwork, or a presentation to professionals, say so — that is work experience in everything but name. A group project where you led the team, managed the deadline, or built the final presentation demonstrates project skills employers actively look for.

Create an experience section from what you have

List each activity with a title, organisation, and dates, then describe it with achievement-style bullets — action verb, task, result — exactly as a job would be described:

  • Volunteering: "Volunteer, Community Food Bank — Packed and distributed food parcels for 60+ households each Saturday; trained three new volunteers on the sorting system."
  • Personal projects: "Built a budgeting spreadsheet used by my family to track monthly expenses; later adapted it for two relatives" — or a blog, a coding project, a small online shop, a YouTube channel. Real output counts.
  • Part-time and family work: Helping in a family business is genuine work. "Assisted in family grocery store — served customers, handled cash, and restocked shelves during peak hours" demonstrates trust, numeracy, and customer skills.
  • Sports and societies: Captaining a team, organising events, or managing a society budget shows leadership and commitment over time.

Never invent employers or inflate titles — a "volunteer" honestly described impresses more than a fake internship, and references checks will expose fabrication instantly.

Build a skills section from real life

Read the job advert and match its requirements to evidence from your life. Software skills (Word, Excel, Google Workspace, social platforms, basic design or editing tools), languages, a driving licence, first-aid or food-hygiene certificates, typing speed, and cash-handling all belong here if the job wants them. For each major skill, the rest of your CV should contain the proof — a skill claimed in the list and demonstrated in a project or activity above it is believable; a skill floating alone is not.

Add a short "Projects" section if you need to fill the page

Students and career starters often have project work that deserves its own heading: coursework projects, freelance pieces, open-source contributions, designs, writing, or anything you made that can be shown. Describe each in two lines — what it was, what tools or skills you used, and the outcome. Where possible, include a link: a portfolio, a GitHub profile, a published article. Tangible output is the beginner's substitute for a job title, and employers respond to it strongly.

What to leave out

  • Your full home address, date of birth, and a photo (unless your country's convention requires one)
  • References — "available on request" wastes a line; employers will ask
  • Long lists of hobbies with no achievement attached — keep hobbies to one line, and only if they show something relevant
  • Anything you cannot discuss confidently in an interview

Cover the gaps with a cover letter

A short CV plus a strong, specific cover letter is a powerful combination for beginners, because the letter lets you connect your coursework and projects directly to this employer's needs and show genuine motivation — the thing entry-level hiring managers care about most. And while you apply, keep building evidence: our guide on how to find a job with no experience lists the fastest ways to add real experience in weeks, not years. Your first CV will not be your best one. It only has to be honest, specific, and clear — that is enough to get your first interview, and the first interview changes everything.

How to Answer "Tell Me About Yourself" in an Interview

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 9 min read

It sounds like small talk, but "tell me about yourself" is the most consequential question in the interview. It usually comes first, it sets the interviewer's impression of you, and it quietly steers the questions that follow. Candidates who ramble through their life story lose the room in the first two minutes. Candidates with a prepared, structured answer take control of the interview from the start. The good news: this is the easiest question to prepare for, because you know it is coming.

What the interviewer actually wants

They do not want your childhood, your hobbies, or a spoken version of your entire CV. They want a professional summary that answers one question: why are you a credible candidate for this role? Specifically, they are listening for your current situation, the experience most relevant to this job, and a reason to believe you want this position rather than any position. Everything in your answer should serve one of those three purposes. If a detail does not, cut it.

The present–past–future formula

The most reliable structure has three parts, in this order:

  1. Present: Your current role or situation, and your headline achievement in it. ("I'm currently a customer service representative at…, where I handle around forty enquiries a day and hold a 98% satisfaction rating.")
  2. Past: The one or two earlier experiences that built the skills this job needs. Keep it brief — this is background, not biography.
  3. Future: Why this role, at this company, is the logical next step. Connect their needs to your direction. This ending is what interviewers remember.

The whole answer should take between ninety seconds and two minutes. Shorter feels underprepared; longer loses attention and eats into the interview.

Example answers

For an experienced candidate:

"I'm currently a team leader at a logistics company, where I supervise a team of eight and coordinate deliveries for around two hundred clients a week. Last year I reorganised our route planning, which cut late deliveries by a quarter. Before that, I spent three years as a warehouse operative, so I've done the ground-level work my team does now, which I think helps me lead it fairly. I'm now looking to move into operations management, and this role interests me because of its scale — the multi-site responsibility is exactly the step I want to take next."

For a graduate or beginner:

"I've just completed my degree in business administration, where I focused on marketing and completed a final-year project analysing social media data for a local retailer. Alongside my studies I volunteered as the social media coordinator for a student society, growing its following to three thousand and promoting events that regularly sold out. That's what confirmed I want to build a career in marketing. Your assistant role appeals to me because it combines content creation with analytics — the two areas where my project and volunteering experience are strongest."

Notice how both examples end in the future, pointed at this specific employer. That final connection is what separates a summary from a story.

Tailor it every time

Prepare one base answer, then adjust the emphasis for each interview. Applying to a role that stresses teamwork? Let your team example carry more weight. A role focused on data? Lead with the analytical achievement. The facts stay the same; the spotlight moves. This takes ten minutes with the job advert open beside you, and it is the same tailoring principle that applies to your resume and cover letter.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Reciting your CV in date order. They have read it. Summarise and interpret it instead.
  • Personal details. Your family, hometown, and hobbies belong in small talk after the offer, not in your professional opening — unless a hobby is genuinely relevant to the role.
  • Speaking badly of your current employer. If your reason for moving comes up, keep it forward-looking, as with all difficult interview questions.
  • Apologising for your background. Career changers and beginners often undermine themselves ("I know I don't have much experience, but…"). Present what you have with confidence; let the interviewer judge its weight.
  • Running long. Practise with a timer. Two focused minutes beat five drifting ones every time.

Adapting your answer for video and panel interviews

The formula does not change on video, but the delivery does: look into the camera rather than at your own image, and keep the answer closer to ninety seconds, because attention fades faster on screen — our video interview guide covers the setup in detail. In a panel interview, direct your opening sentence to the person who asked, then let your gaze move naturally around the panel as you continue, finishing back with the questioner. If the interviewer follows up with "tell me more about that project," treat it as good news: they are asking you to expand the part of your story that interested them, which is exactly the conversation your answer was designed to start. Prepare one layer of extra detail for each claim in your summary — a figure, a timeframe, a result — so any follow-up can be answered with specifics rather than repetition.

How to practise

Write your answer as bullet points, not a script — a memorised script sounds flat and collapses if the interviewer interrupts. Say it aloud several times until the structure feels natural, then record yourself once and listen for filler words and rushed sections. Practise the first sentence most of all: if your opening line comes out clean and confident, the rest of the answer — and the interview — tends to follow. Master this question and you will walk into every interview with the first two minutes already won.

How to Write a Resignation Letter (With Examples)

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 10 min read

A resignation letter is a short document with a long memory. It sits in your personnel file, it is often the last written impression you leave, and industries are smaller than they feel — the manager you resign to today may be asked for a reference, or become your client, or interview you again in five years. The goal of the letter is therefore simple: state your decision clearly, give correct notice, offer a professional handover, and express genuine gratitude. Nothing more is required, and anything more is usually a mistake. This guide covers the format, the timing, and three complete examples for different situations.

Before the letter: the conversation comes first

Your manager should hear the news from you, in person or by video call — never from a letter arriving without warning, and never from colleagues you told first. Book a short meeting, state your decision calmly, and then hand over or send the letter the same day as the formal record. Check your contract before the conversation so you know your exact notice period, any rules about working it, and what happens to unused leave. If you have negotiated a new offer, make sure it is confirmed in writing before you resign — the sequence matters, as our salary negotiation guide explains.

What every resignation letter must include

  • Your name, the date, and your manager's name
  • A clear statement that you are resigning from your position
  • Your final working day, calculated from your contractual notice period
  • A brief offer to help with the handover of your duties
  • A short, sincere expression of thanks
  • Your signature (for a printed letter) or full name (for email)

That is the complete list. Notice what is absent: your reasons in detail, your new employer (optional — share it verbally if asked, but it is not required in the letter), grievances, and apologies. One page, usually under two hundred words, is ideal.

Example 1: The standard professional resignation

Dear Ms. Patel,

Please accept this letter as formal notice of my resignation from my position as Administrative Assistant, effective four weeks from today. My final working day will be Friday, 18 December 2026.

I am grateful for the opportunities I have had here over the past three years, and particularly for your support in developing my skills in office management. I have learned a great deal that I will carry into the next stage of my career.

I will do everything I can during my notice period to hand over my duties smoothly, including completing my current projects and preparing notes for whoever takes over my responsibilities.

Thank you again for your guidance and for a rewarding three years.

Sincerely,
Daniel Wright

Example 2: A short resignation by email

When your workplace runs on email, a concise message with the subject line "Resignation — [Your Name]" is perfectly acceptable:

Dear James,

I am writing to resign from my role as Sales Associate. In line with my contract, my last working day will be 30 November 2026.

Thank you for the opportunities and support you have given me during my two years with the company. I appreciate everything I have learned here.

I am happy to help train my replacement and hand over my accounts during my notice period.

Best regards,
Sofia Marino

Example 3: Resigning for a career change or relocation

Dear Mr. Thompson,

After much consideration, I have decided to resign from my position as Customer Service Representative, with my final day being 15 January 2027, in accordance with my notice period.

This was not an easy decision. I am relocating to be closer to family and will be changing direction in my career, but I want to emphasise how much I have valued working with this team. The training and trust I received here gave me the confidence to take this step.

I will prepare full handover documentation and am glad to help train my successor before I leave.

With sincere thanks,
Michael Chen

If you are resigning to change fields entirely, our guide on how to switch careers at 30 or 40 will help you plan what comes next.

What never belongs in a resignation letter

  • Criticism of your manager, colleagues, or the company. However justified, it achieves nothing and is remembered forever. Raise genuine issues in a separate, calm exit conversation if you wish — or not at all.
  • A list of grievances or an ultimatum. If you would stay for a better offer, that is a negotiation to have before resigning, not a threat inside a resignation letter.
  • Excessive apology or self-blame. Resigning is a normal professional act, not a betrayal.
  • Promises you will not keep about handover or availability after your last day. Offer what you can genuinely deliver.

Your notice period: finish as well as you started

The letter opens your exit; your behaviour during the notice period defines it. Complete your handover properly, document your recurring tasks, stay positive with colleagues, and resist the temptation to coast. People remember last impressions disproportionately — and the reference your manager writes, the introduction they make for you, and the welcome you would receive if you ever returned all depend on these final weeks. Write the letter well, work the notice well, and you leave with something more valuable than a clean file: a network of people who will speak well of you for the rest of your career.

How to Prepare for a Video Interview

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 10 min read

Video interviews are now a permanent part of hiring — often the first round, sometimes the entire process. They test the same things as in-person interviews, plus one extra: how professionally you present yourself through a screen. Candidates lose video interviews to bad lighting, echoing audio, ringing phones, and technology they never tested, long before their answers are judged. The good news is that nearly every video-specific problem can be eliminated with an hour of preparation. Here is the complete routine.

Step 1: Test the technology the day before, not the hour before

Download and install the platform the employer uses (Zoom, Teams, Google Meet, or their own system) as soon as you receive the invitation. Open it, check that your camera and microphone are recognised, and run a test call with a friend or family member. Confirm three things on that call: they can hear you clearly, they can see you clearly, and your internet connection holds a stable picture. Update the software if it asks — updates forced at interview time are a classic disaster. Charge your laptop or plug it in, and have a backup plan: the meeting link on your phone, with the employer's phone number saved in case everything fails and you need to call and explain like a professional.

Step 2: Build your set — background, lighting, camera position

Sit facing your main light source — a window in front of you is ideal; a window behind you turns you into a silhouette. If natural light is not available, place a lamp in front of you, slightly to one side. Raise the camera to eye level using books or a box; a laptop sitting low on a desk creates an unflattering upward angle and a wandering gaze. Your background should be plain and tidy: a bare wall, a neat bookshelf, or a blurred or virtual background if your space is genuinely unsuitable. Sit roughly an arm's length from the camera so your head and shoulders fill the frame comfortably, and check the picture once more in the platform's preview before you join.

Step 3: Sound matters more than picture

Interviewers forgive a soft picture; they struggle through bad audio. Choose the quietest room you have, close windows and doors, and tell anyone at home exactly when you will be live. Wired earbuds or a headset with a microphone placed near your mouth will almost always sound clearer than a laptop microphone across a room. Test by recording yourself answering a question and listening back — if you hear echo, move to a smaller room with soft furnishings, which absorb sound naturally.

Step 4: Dress and prepare exactly as you would in person

Wear the full interview outfit, not just the visible half — it changes how you sit, speak, and think, and you may need to stand unexpectedly. Our guide on what to wear to a job interview covers choosing the right level of formality. On your desk, keep only: a glass of water, a pen, paper for notes, a printed copy of your resume, and the job advert. Close every other application, silence your phone and computer notifications, and pause anything that syncs, uploads, or updates in the background.

Step 5: Master on-screen body language

Look at the camera lens when you answer, not at your own image — that is where eye contact lives on video. Glance at the interviewer's image when they speak, then return to the lens for your answer. Sit up, keep gestures small and within the frame, and nod and react visibly while listening, because video flattens the subtle signals that show engagement in person. Speak slightly more slowly than usual and pause briefly before answering: connections carry a small delay, and talking over the interviewer repeatedly is the most common video-interview irritant. A genuine smile at the start and end carries further on screen than you would expect.

Step 6: Prepare your answers and your environment for questions

The questions themselves will be the familiar ones — prepare with our list of 20 common interview questions and your structured answer to "tell me about yourself". One advantage of video: discreet notes are acceptable. A sticky note beside the camera with your three key achievements and the questions you want to ask is invisible to the interviewer and genuinely useful. Keep notes minimal — reading paragraphs aloud is obvious on camera and sounds worse than a thoughtful pause.

When things go wrong (and how to recover)

  • The connection freezes: Stay calm, say "I think the connection dropped — could you repeat the last question?" Interviewers judge recovery, not the glitch.
  • Audio fails completely: Use the chat to explain, then suggest continuing by phone. Having the number ready, as in Step 1, turns a crisis into a demonstration of preparation.
  • Noise or interruption at home: Apologise once, briefly, mute while you resolve it, and continue. Do not over-apologise for the next ten minutes.
  • You are cut off mid-answer: Rejoin promptly and pick up with a summary sentence — "As I was saying, the result was…" — rather than starting over.

Afterwards, send the same thank-you and follow-up email you would after an in-person interview, within a few hours while you are fresh in their minds. A video interview rewards exactly what hiring always rewards — preparation — it just makes preparation visible. Test your setup, set your scene, and let your answers do the rest.

How to Find a Job With No Experience

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 11 min read

"Entry-level job, two years of experience required." If you have seen that advert, you know the frustration of the beginner's trap: you need experience to get a job, and a job to get experience. The trap is real, but it is not airtight. Employers hire inexperienced people constantly — they simply hire the ones who present the best evidence of ability and reliability. This guide shows you where beginner-friendly opportunities actually are, how to build credible experience quickly, and how to apply in a way that gets replies instead of silence.

First, reframe what "experience" means

Employers do not need you to have held the same job title before. They need confidence that you can do the tasks, show up reliably, learn quickly, and behave professionally. Evidence for those things comes from many places: coursework and training, volunteering, internships, part-time and family work, personal projects, sports, and community roles. A candidate who has run a small online shop from their bedroom has genuinely practised customer service, marketing, money handling, and problem-solving. Your first task is to inventory your own evidence honestly — our guide on how to write a CV with no experience walks through exactly how to present it.

Where beginner-friendly jobs actually hide

  • Sectors built on entry-level hiring: retail, hospitality, customer service, care work, warehousing and logistics, call centres, and administration constantly train beginners, because their whole staffing model depends on it.
  • Apprenticeships, traineeships, and internships: these exist precisely for people without experience, pay (or should) at least a training wage, and often convert into permanent roles.
  • Small local businesses: independent shops, trades, salons, cafes, and offices often hire through a conversation rather than a portal — and many never advertise formally at all.
  • Temporary and agency work: agencies place beginners into short assignments where reliability is the main requirement; good temps are offered permanent roles at a remarkable rate.
  • Seasonal hiring: retail at holidays, tourism in summer, tax and accounting firms in filing season, and events year-round all lower their experience bars when they need people fast.

Build experience fast — in weeks, not years

While you search, deliberately manufacture the evidence your CV lacks. Volunteer one or two days a week in a role related to your target field — a charity shop for retail, a community centre office for administration, a local sports club's social media for marketing. Take a free or low-cost certificate course in the tools your target jobs name (spreadsheets, bookkeeping software, food hygiene, first aid, a coding language) so your applications can list them truthfully. Create one tangible project: a portfolio of designs, a small website, a set of practice bookkeeping accounts, a translated document. And offer freelance or family-business help wherever it is real. Four to six weeks of this transforms a CV from "nothing yet" to "consistently active and building skills" — which is the story employers actually buy.

Use your network — most first jobs come through people

A large share of entry-level hiring never reaches a job board. Tell everyone you know — family, friends, former teachers, teammates, neighbours — specifically what you are looking for: "I'm looking for office or admin work, full-time, and I have strong computer skills" gets passed on; "I need a job" does not. Follow up introductions promptly and gratefully. Optimise your LinkedIn profile even as a beginner, connect with people you genuinely know, and let your settings tell recruiters you are open to work. Being recommended by a trusted person bypasses the experience filter entirely, because the recommendation itself is the evidence.

Apply like it matters — because volume without tailoring fails

Fifty identical applications lose to ten tailored ones. For each application: mirror the advert's language in your CV's skills section, write a short, specific cover letter explaining why this company and how your evidence matches their needs, and double-check every instruction in the advert — beginners are often filtered out for missing attachments or unanswered questions, not for inexperience. Apply early in an advert's life where possible, and keep a simple spreadsheet of where you applied, when, and what happened, so follow-ups do not slip.

Prepare to prove it in the interview

When the interview comes — and with this approach, it will — expect to be tested on attitude and examples rather than track record. Prepare stories from your volunteering, projects, and coursework using the STAR structure in our interview questions guide, and rehearse a confident answer to "tell me about yourself" that frames your short history as a deliberate build-up to this role. Employers interviewing beginners are asking one question underneath all the others: "Will this person show up, learn fast, and be pleasant to work with?" Every example you give should answer yes.

Stay in the game

Job hunting without experience is a numbers-and-persistence exercise, and rejection at this stage usually means "not yet," not "not you." Set a sustainable weekly rhythm — a set number of tailored applications, one networking action, one skill-building session — and review monthly what is producing responses. Adjust your CV toward whatever gets replies. Everyone's career starts with a first yes from someone willing to take a chance. Make yourself the easiest beginner to say yes to: evidenced, tailored, recommended, and visibly still improving. That first role will not be your dream job. It will be the foundation every later job is built on.
