How to Explain a Gap in Your CV

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 9 min read

Career gaps are far more common than most applicants realise. Redundancy, raising children, caring for a relative, illness, study, travel, a business that did not work out, a difficult job market — hiring managers have seen every one of these, usually in their own families. What makes employers hesitate is rarely the gap itself. It is an unexplained gap, or a candidate who becomes defensive about it. Handled briefly and honestly, most gaps shrink to a minor detail in an application. This guide shows you how to present yours on your CV, in a cover letter, and in the interview room.

The golden rule: brief, honest, forward-looking

Every explanation in this guide follows the same shape: state the reason in one plain sentence, mention anything relevant you did during the period, and move the conversation to your readiness for the role now. Employers need to know three things — what happened (in outline), that it is resolved or managed, and that you are ready to work. They do not need details, apologies, or a defence. The more ordinary you make it sound, the more ordinary it becomes.

On the CV itself

Do not try to hide a gap by fiddling with dates — extending a job by months is a falsification that reference checks routinely expose, and it converts a small issue into a dismissal-level one. Instead, account for the time honestly with a simple line in your career history, written like any other entry:

  • "2024 – 2025: Full-time carer for a family member. Maintained bookkeeping skills through an online certification completed in 2025."
  • "2023 – 2024: Career break to raise my children. Volunteered two days a week at my children's school office, handling scheduling and records."
  • "2025: Redundancy following company restructure. Completed a project management course and freelance consulting projects while job searching."
  • "2022 – 2023: Travel and study. Worked in hospitality roles in two countries and completed an intermediate language qualification."

If the gap involved illness, you are not obliged to share medical details — "a period of ill health, now resolved" is complete and sufficient. For shorter gaps of a few months, years-only dates on older roles are a normal CV convention, but be ready to give months honestly if asked directly.

In the cover letter: one sentence, placed well

If the gap is recent or long, address it in your cover letter in a single sentence within the paragraph about your background — not as the opening, and not as the focus. For example: "Following a two-year break to care for my father, I am returning to administration with refreshed certification in [software] and three months of recent volunteer office experience." Placed between your achievements and your enthusiasm for the role, the gap becomes one fact in a larger, positive story rather than the story itself.

In the interview: the two-sentence answer

Expect the question and prepare a calm, two-sentence answer, rehearsed aloud so it comes out without hesitation or over-explanation:

"After my role was made redundant in 2024, I took the opportunity to care for my mother during her recovery and completed an online diploma in bookkeeping. She's now fully recovered, my qualification is finished, and I'm keen to get back into finance work — which is why this role caught my eye."

Then stop. Candidates damage themselves by continuing — adding justifications, criticising the former employer, or apologising repeatedly. Answer, pause, and let the interviewer move on; they almost always will. Our interview questions guide covers this question among the other common ones you should prepare for.

Fill the gap before it fills the conversation

If you are currently in a gap, the strongest move is to shrink it with present-tense activity. Volunteering, a short course, freelance projects, or part-time work — even a few hours a week — changes your story from "has been out of work" to "is currently doing X and looking for the right role." It also refreshes your skills, your references, and your confidence, all of which show in interviews. The strategies in our guide on finding a job with no experience apply almost word for word to returning after a gap.

Special situations: study, redundancy, and starting out

Some gaps need one extra line of handling. Time spent studying is the easiest — name the qualification and treat it as the investment it was. Redundancy deserves the plainest possible framing: the role was eliminated, it affected a team or a whole department, and it says nothing about your performance; if your former employer will confirm that in a reference, mention it. And if your gap is at the very start of your career — the months after education that stretch longer than planned — fill the story with whatever you built during them: courses, volunteering, freelance attempts, family responsibilities. Employers understand slow starts in a difficult market far better than they understand silence about them, and a candidate who used the time visibly is demonstrating exactly the initiative they hire for.

What never works

  • Lying about dates or inventing employment. The risk is total: one reference call ends the application and sometimes the career move.
  • A purely functional CV that hides all dates. Recruiters notice the omission instantly and assume the worst version of the story.
  • Bitterness about the cause — a former employer, the economy, an ex-manager. Interviewers side with the person not in the room, because one day that could be them.
  • Oversharing personal or medical detail. Outline is enough; you owe an employer clarity, not your private life.

A gap explained in one honest sentence, surrounded by evidence of what you can do now, stops being the headline of your application. Prepare your sentence, keep building present-tense evidence, and walk into the interview ready to talk about the future. That is where employers want the conversation to go — take it there.

How to Write a Professional Email at Work

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 10 min read

Email is where most of your professional reputation is actually built. Colleagues who rarely see you work will judge your competence, reliability, and attitude largely from the messages you send — and those messages live forever, forwarded and searchable long after you have forgotten them. The good news is that professional email follows a simple, learnable structure. Master it, and your emails will be opened sooner, understood faster, and answered more often.

The subject line: a headline, not a label

Your subject line decides whether the email is opened now, later, or never. It should tell the reader what the email is about and, where relevant, what you need and by when. Compare:

  • Weak: "Report" / "Question" / "Hello"
  • Strong: "Q3 sales report attached — no action needed"
  • Strong: "Approval needed by Thursday: new supplier contract"
  • Strong: "Meeting moved to 2 pm Friday — agenda attached"

Keep it under about eight words, put the most important word early, and update the subject when a long thread changes topic. If the email needs action, say so in the subject — busy people triage by exactly that.

The structure that gets answers

Almost every work email works in five short parts:

  1. Greeting: "Hi Sarah," for colleagues; "Dear Mr. Ahmed," for formal or first-contact emails. When unsure, slightly too formal beats slightly too casual.
  2. Opening line: One sentence of context or goodwill — why you are writing. ("Following up on Tuesday's meeting about the delivery schedule…")
  3. The point: State what you need or what you are reporting, early — not buried in paragraph three. Busy readers scan the first lines.
  4. The detail: Background, options, or evidence, kept as short as the reader needs. Use bullets or numbered lists for anything with more than two items.
  5. The close: A specific call to action ("Could you confirm by Friday whether option B works?") and a courteous sign-off ("Best regards," "Kind regards," "Thanks,").

One topic per email. Two unrelated requests in one message usually means one of them gets ignored or lost. If you have two subjects, send two emails with two clear subject lines.

Tone: professional means clear and warm, not stiff

Modern professional email is not legal language. Write in complete sentences, use contractions naturally, and be direct without being blunt. Read your draft once asking: "How would this sound read aloud in a flat voice?" — because that is roughly how recipients hear it. Exclamation marks: one per email at most. Capital letters for emphasis read as shouting; use bold sparingly instead. Emojis belong only where your workplace culture clearly uses them and you know the recipient well. When in doubt — first emails, senior recipients, anything sensitive — leave them out.

Example: requesting something

Subject: Approval needed by Thursday: updated delivery schedule

Hi Martin,

Following the supplier delay we discussed, I've revised the delivery schedule for next month (attached). The main change is that the Bristol deliveries move from Mondays to Wednesdays.

Could you approve the new schedule by Thursday? The warehouse team needs it by Friday to plan the rota.

Thanks for your help,
Priya

Notice the anatomy: context in one line, the change stated plainly, the request with a deadline and a reason. Four short paragraphs, nothing wasted.

Example: delivering bad news

Subject: Project Atlas — revised completion date

Hi team,

I need to let you know that the Atlas report will be completed on 12 December rather than 5 December. Our data provider delivered the final figures a week late, and I don't want to rush the checks that make the report reliable.

The draft sections are already with you, and I'll share the completed analysis the moment the checks finish. I'm sorry for the disruption to your planning — please let me know if the new date creates problems I can help with.

Best regards,
Tom

Bad news emails work when they are early, honest about the cause without blaming others, specific about the new plan, and brief. The worst version — silence until the deadline passes — is also the most common.

The checks before you press send

  • Recipients: Is everyone on this email supposed to see it? Check before using Reply All — and think twice before adding CCs, which can read as escalation.
  • Attachments: If the email says "attached," is it actually attached? Mentioning it in the first line makes you check.
  • Names and facts: Correct spellings of names, correct dates, correct figures. Errors here undo the professionalism of everything else.
  • The forward test: Assume this email will be forwarded to your manager and the person it discusses. If that thought makes you uneasy, rewrite.
  • Emotional drafts: If you are angry, write the draft, save it, and re-read it after a break — or the next morning. Never send the first version of an emotional email. This rule alone has saved countless working relationships, including with difficult bosses.

Professional email is a daily habit, not an occasional performance. Clear subjects, early points, specific requests, and a thirty-second check before sending will put your writing ahead of most of the inbox — and the reputation that follows will quietly power everything from your personal brand to your next promotion case.

How to Handle a Difficult Boss Professionally

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 11 min read

A difficult manager can turn a job you enjoy into a daily source of stress — and how you handle the relationship will shape your reputation, your references, and often your next move. "Difficult" takes many forms: the micromanager who checks everything, the absent boss who gives no direction, the credit-taker, the one whose expectations change without warning. Each needs a slightly different response, but all of them reward the same approach: stay calm, get specific, document facts, and protect your professionalism at all times. This guide gives you strategies for the common types, how to have the hard conversation, and how to recognise when the right answer is to leave well.

First, diagnose the behaviour, not the person

"My boss is impossible" is a feeling, not a workable problem. Translate it into observable behaviour: "My manager changes priorities without telling me, then criticises missed deadlines." "My manager reviews my drafts three times before anything can be sent." Specific behaviours can be managed, negotiated, or documented; personalities cannot. This distinction also keeps you honest — sometimes what feels like a difficult boss is a stretched boss, an unclear brief, or a simple mismatch in working style that a conversation genuinely fixes.

Strategies by type

The micromanager

Micromanagement usually comes from anxiety, not malice. Feed it information before it asks: brief proactive updates ("Quick note: the report is drafted, I'm checking figures this afternoon, you'll have it by 10 tomorrow") remove the uncertainty that drives the checking. Agree checkpoints explicitly — "I'll update you at draft stage and final stage" — and then meet every one. Trust with micromanagers is earned in small, kept promises, and many loosen their grip noticeably once a pattern of reliability is established.

The absent or unclear boss

When direction is missing, create it. After any conversation, send a short email summarising your understanding: "Just confirming I'll prioritise A and B this week and pause C — let me know if you'd rank them differently." This gives them an easy chance to correct you and creates a written record that you sought clarity. Ask questions that force prioritisation: "Both are due Friday — which matters more if I can only complete one to a high standard?"

The credit-taker

Protect your visibility without accusing anyone. Share your work in writing — progress emails to wider groups, updates in team meetings, documents with your name and date on them — so your contribution exists on the record naturally. Copying relevant colleagues on key deliverables is not politics; it is normal professional communication, and it quietly makes credit-taking much harder. The habits in our guide to building a personal brand at work are your long-term insurance here.

The constantly critical boss

Separate the signal from the delivery. Ask for specifics — "Which part of the report fell short, and what would good look like next time?" — and write down agreed standards so criticism can be measured against them. Feedback delivered harshly can still contain usable information; extract it, apply what's valid, and let the tone go. If criticism is personal rather than about work, that is a different and more serious matter, covered below.

Have the conversation — carefully

If a pattern persists, a calm, private conversation is worth attempting before anything escalates. Choose a neutral moment, use specific examples, describe impact rather than character, and propose a solution:

"I'd like to talk about how we handle project deadlines. Twice this month the priority changed mid-week without my hearing about it, and I ended up delivering the wrong piece of work first. Could we have a ten-minute check-in on Monday mornings to confirm the week's priorities? I think that would stop it happening."

Note the structure: behaviour, impact, request. No labels ("you're disorganised"), no history-dredging, no ultimatums. Many managers genuinely do not know the effect they are having, and a well-run conversation improves things more often than people expect. Follow the professional communication principles in our guide on communication skills at work.

Document, quietly and factually

Keep a private record of significant incidents: dates, what was said or done, who was present, and any written evidence. Store it outside work systems if your policies allow, and write it as facts, not feelings. Documentation is not about building a weapon; it is about accuracy if a pattern ever needs to be raised formally with HR or a senior manager — and memory alone is unreliable under stress. Continue confirming important verbal instructions by email as a matter of routine.

Know the line: difficult versus unacceptable

Demanding, disorganised, or socially clumsy management is difficult. Bullying, discrimination, harassment, being asked to do something illegal or unsafe, or retaliation for raising concerns is unacceptable — and different rules apply. In those cases, use your organisation's formal channels: HR, grievance procedures, union representatives, or the external employment advice services in your country. Document thoroughly, keep copies, and take advice before resigning in the heat of a moment. Your health and safety outrank any job.

And know when to leave well

Sometimes you will do everything right and nothing will change, because the problem is the organisation's culture rather than one fixable habit. Staying indefinitely in a role that damages your confidence and health is not professionalism; it is slow harm. Leaving well is a skill too: line up your next move first using our guides on resumes and interviews, keep your performance clean to the end, and resign gracefully with a proper resignation letter. You can handle a difficult boss professionally for a season. You are not obliged to build your whole career around one.

How to Improve Your Communication Skills at Work

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 10 min read

Ask employers what separates the people they promote from the people they do not, and communication appears near the top of almost every answer — ahead of most technical skills. That is because nearly every expensive workplace failure is a communication failure in disguise: the misunderstood brief, the unspoken concern, the update nobody sent. Communication is not a talent you are born with; it is a set of habits, each of which can be practised deliberately. This guide covers the five that matter most at work and how to build each one.

1. Listen like it is your job — because it is

Most people listen in order to reply. Effective communicators listen in order to understand. The habits are simple and rare: let the other person finish without interrupting; ask one clarifying question before giving your view ("When you say the report felt rushed, do you mean the analysis or the writing?"); and summarise what you heard before responding ("So the priority is accuracy over speed this time — have I got that right?"). That thirty-second summary prevents half of all workplace misunderstandings, and it makes colleagues feel heard, which makes them far more willing to hear you. In meetings, take brief notes — it signals attention and gives you accurate material to act on.

2. Speak in structure, not in streams

When you speak — in a meeting, an update, or an answer to your manager — put the point first and the background second. "The launch will slip by a week because the supplier is late. Here's what I propose…" respects everyone's time and lands your message before attention wanders. Long preambles cause listeners to guess your point, often wrongly. A useful discipline for updates is the three-part frame: where things stand, what has changed, what you need or propose next. Practise it in low-stakes moments — team check-ins, status calls — and it will be there when the stakes rise, in presentations and interviews alike.

3. Write so you cannot be misunderstood

Most workplace communication is now written — email, chat, documents — and writing exposes unclear thinking mercilessly. The core rules: one topic per message, the request early, short paragraphs, and specific language ("by Thursday at noon" beats "soon"; "the Henderson contract" beats "that thing"). Re-read anything important once from the recipient's chair: what do they know, what do they not know, what will they do after reading this? Our guide on how to write a professional email at work gives the full method with examples. In chat tools, remember that brevity reads as coldness — a complete sentence and an occasional acknowledgement ("Thanks — got it, will do") costs nothing and warms everything.

4. Speak up in meetings, usefully

Silence in meetings is often read as disengagement, however hard you are working outside them. You do not need to dominate; you need to contribute visibly and usefully. Prepare one point or question before every meeting — reading the agenda and deciding your view in advance removes the pressure of improvising. Ask the question others are silently holding ("Could we clarify who owns the next step?"), summarise progress when discussion circles, and volunteer for small visible pieces: presenting your section, reporting back next week. If speaking in a group is genuinely hard for you, start with written contributions — a pre-meeting note or a follow-up summary — and build from there. Visibility built this way is also how colleagues come to associate your name with competence, the heart of personal brand at work.

5. Give and receive feedback without drama

Feedback is where communication skills pay or cost the most. When giving it: be specific, be prompt, describe behaviour and impact rather than personality, and include the path forward. "In yesterday's client call, the figures were quoted from memory and two were wrong — let's agree to have the sheet open next time" improves work. "You're careless with numbers" only damages the relationship. When receiving feedback, resist the instant defence: listen fully, ask for an example if it is vague, thank the person, and decide later what to act on. People who receive feedback gracefully get more of it — and early feedback is one of the fastest accelerators of a career. If the feedback comes from a manager whose style is harsh, our guide on handling a difficult boss shows how to extract the value safely.

Adapt to your audience

The same message needs different shapes for different listeners. Senior leaders usually want the conclusion, the impact, and the decision needed — detail on request. Technical colleagues want precision and reasoning. Clients want reassurance, plain language, and clear next steps. New team members need context you may have forgotten they lack. Before any significant communication, ask one question: "What does this person need from me, and what do they already know?" Thirty seconds of audience-thinking improves more messages than any amount of editing afterwards.

A simple practice plan

  • Week 1–2: Summarise before responding in every significant conversation. Notice how many misunderstandings die at birth.
  • Week 3–4: Put the point first in every update, spoken and written. Prepare one contribution before each meeting.
  • Month 2: Ask two colleagues you trust one question: "What's one thing I could do to communicate more clearly?" Act visibly on what they say.
  • Ongoing: Keep a small file of messages and presentations that went well, and review what made them work before your next big one.

Communication compounds. Each clearer email, calmer meeting, and better-handled feedback conversation adds to a reputation for being easy to work with and easy to trust — and that reputation, more than any single skill, is what carries people into promotions and leadership. Start with listening this week; the rest builds from there.

How to Ask for a Raise by Email (With Examples)

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 10 min read

Sometimes the pay conversation starts in writing. Your manager works remotely, your company's review process runs through formal requests, or you simply express yourself better on paper than in a high-stakes meeting. A well-written raise email has real advantages: it presents your evidence in an organised form, gives your manager something concrete to forward to whoever approves budgets, and creates a record of the request. This guide explains when email is the right channel, how to structure the message, and gives you three complete templates to adapt.

First: should this be an email at all?

Email works best as an opener — a way to present your case and request a meeting to discuss it — rather than as the entire negotiation. Most managers cannot approve a raise in a reply; they need to check budgets and often get sign-off from above. So the strongest raise emails end with a request for a conversation, not a demand for an answer. Email is the right first step when your manager is remote or travelling, when your organisation formally invites written requests before review season, or when a face-to-face ask has been repeatedly postponed. If your relationship is good and you share an office, a short email asking for a meeting "to discuss my compensation at the review" plus your evidence attached is the professional middle path.

Before you write: gather your case

No template can rescue a raise request with nothing behind it. Before drafting, assemble the same material described in our promotion guide:

  • Your results: measurable achievements since your last raise or since you joined — revenue, savings, projects delivered, quality improvements
  • Your expanded scope: responsibilities you have taken on that were not in your original role
  • Your market evidence: the going rate for your role and experience in your area, from salary surveys and comparable job adverts
  • Your number: a specific figure or range you are asking for, consistent with that research

Timing matters too. Send your request when your recent results are visible, ahead of budget and review cycles where possible — and not during a company crisis, a redundancy round, or the week your manager delivers bad results.

The structure of an effective raise email

  1. Subject: Clear and neutral — "Request to discuss my compensation" or "Salary review request — [Your Name]".
  2. Opening: Brief goodwill and the purpose of the email in one line.
  3. Evidence: Three or four bullet points of results and expanded responsibilities, quantified wherever possible.
  4. Market context: One sentence anchoring your request in research, not personal need.
  5. The ask: Your specific figure, stated once, calmly.
  6. The close: A request to discuss in a meeting, and thanks.

Notice what is absent: your rent, your bills, your colleague's salary, or any hint of a threat. Raises are granted for value and market reality, never for personal expenses — keep the email entirely on the first two.

Template 1: The standard raise request

Subject: Request to discuss my compensation

Hi Sarah,

I'd like to request a review of my salary. I've really enjoyed the past two years in this role, and I believe my contributions have grown significantly in that time:

• I led the migration to the new booking system, which reduced processing time by 30%.
• I now train all new starters in the department — six people this year.
• Customer satisfaction scores for my accounts have averaged 96% over the last twelve months.

Based on my research into similar roles in our region, and the additional responsibilities I've taken on, I'd like to request an increase to £34,000. I'm happy to discuss the details whenever suits you — perhaps we could find thirty minutes next week?

Thank you for considering it,
Emma

Template 2: After taking on a bigger role informally

Subject: Salary review — expanded responsibilities

Hi David,

Since March, I've been covering the senior coordinator's duties alongside my own — supervising two assistants, managing the supplier accounts, and presenting the monthly figures to the leadership team. I'm glad to be doing the work, and the feedback has been positive.

As the arrangement has become permanent, I'd like my salary to reflect the role I'm now performing. Comparable senior coordinator roles locally are advertised between £36,000 and £39,000, and I'd like to request £37,000.

Could we meet in the next couple of weeks to discuss? I can bring a summary of the work I've taken on.

Best regards,
James

Template 3: The short version, ahead of review season

Subject: Ahead of my review — compensation

Hi Anna,

Ahead of my annual review next month, I wanted to flag that I'd like compensation to be part of our discussion. This year I delivered the onboarding project six weeks early and took over reporting for the whole team, and I'd like to request a raise to £41,000 in line with the market rate for this role.

I can share the full details in our review meeting — I just wanted you to have it in mind beforehand.

Many thanks,
Laura

After you send: the follow-through

Give your manager reasonable time — a week, or until the meeting you requested. If you hear nothing, one polite follow-up is appropriate ("Just checking you received my email about a salary review — happy to work around your schedule for a meeting"). In the meeting itself, use the calm, evidence-based approach from our salary negotiation guide: let them respond, negotiate the whole package if the figure is fixed, and confirm any agreement by email afterwards. If the answer is no, ask the two questions that turn a no into a plan: what specifically would need to change, and when can we review it again? Then get that date in writing. A raise email is not a gamble — it is the documented start of a process. Write it with evidence, send it at the right moment, and follow through like a professional.

What to Wear to a Job Interview

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 9 min read

Interviewers form their first impression of you before you answer a single question — and a significant part of that impression is what you are wearing. This is not about fashion or expense. It is about sending one message clearly: "I understand this workplace, I respect this opportunity, and I paid attention." The right outfit removes a distraction and lets your answers do the work. The wrong one becomes the thing the panel remembers. Here is how to get it right for any industry.

The golden rule: one step smarter than the daily dress code

The most reliable formula in interview dressing is to dress one level more formally than employees dress on a normal day in that workplace. Interviewing at a bank where staff wear suits? Wear a suit. At a design studio where people wear smart casual? Wear a blazer, clean trousers or a smart dress, and polished shoes — not a three-piece suit, which would signal you do not understand the culture. At a tech company where engineers wear jeans and hoodies? Smart trousers or dark, neat jeans with a proper shirt or blouse and a blazer is usually the sweet spot. The aim is to look like the best-dressed version of someone who already works there.

How to research what "one step smarter" means

  • Check the company's own material: team photos on their website and social media show the real dress culture better than any policy document.
  • Ask the recruiter: "Is there a dress code you'd recommend for the interview?" is a normal, sensible question that no hiring manager minds answering.
  • Consider the role: client-facing, finance, law, and public-sector roles skew formal; creative, tech, and start-up roles skew relaxed — but the interview itself is always at the smarter end of a company's range.
  • When genuinely unsure, go formal. Being slightly overdressed is forgiven in seconds; being underdressed is remembered all day.

Outfit formulas by dress code

Formal (law, finance, senior corporate, government)

A well-fitting suit in navy, charcoal, or dark grey with a light shirt or blouse, a conservative tie if you wear one, and clean, polished closed shoes. For skirt or dress suits, keep hemlines at or near the knee. Everything pressed, nothing tight or uncomfortable — you will be sitting, standing, and possibly walking between rooms.

Business casual (most offices, education, healthcare administration, retail management)

Smart trousers or a skirt with a shirt or blouse and a blazer, or a neat dress with a cardigan or jacket. Ties are optional in most business-casual settings. Shoes should be clean and closed-toe. This is the category where fit and condition matter more than formality — immaculate smart casual beats a sloppy suit.

Smart casual (creative industries, start-ups, hospitality, media)

Dark, unripped jeans or chinos with a shirt, blouse, or fine knit, plus a blazer or smart jacket to lift the whole outfit. Clean, minimalist trainers can work in genuinely casual creative workplaces, but proper shoes are the safer default for a first meeting. Avoid shorts, sportswear, large logos, and anything you would wear to a festival.

Trades, healthcare, and practical roles

If the interview includes a site visit or practical test, dress neatly and safely: clean work-appropriate clothing, no dangling jewellery or loose sleeves, and bring or wear any safety footwear the employer mentions. Cleanliness and readiness signal professionalism in these settings more than formality does.

The details interviewers actually notice

  • Shoes: Clean and in good repair. Scuffed, dirty shoes are the single most noticed detail in interview dress surveys.
  • Fit and comfort: Clothes you fidget with, tug at, or cannot sit comfortably in will distract you and them. Try the full outfit on, sitting down, before the day.
  • Grooming: Clean hair, trimmed nails, and minimal, fresh scent — heavy perfume or aftershave in a small interview room is a genuine problem.
  • Accessories: Keep jewellery quiet and minimal; remove anything noisy. A simple watch and a tidy bag or folder for your documents complete the picture.
  • Preparation details: Iron or steam everything the night before, check for missing buttons and loose threads, and lay the outfit out so the morning is calm. For video interviews, the same standards apply to everything the camera sees — see our video interview guide.

Planning for travel, weather, and the unexpected

Work out your route and aim to arrive fifteen minutes early, with your outfit protected accordingly: an umbrella if rain threatens, a brush or lint roller in your bag, and a minute in the restroom or lobby to check your appearance before you are announced. If you are travelling straight from another job, change fully rather than trying to upgrade a work uniform with a jacket — the half-changed look is worse than either option. And if something goes genuinely wrong — a train cancelled, a spill on your shirt — phone ahead, explain briefly, and walk in composed anyway. Employers judge the recovery, and a candidate who handles a small crisis calmly has just demonstrated a quality no outfit can show.

What to avoid

  • Brand-new shoes or an outfit you have never worn — discomfort shows on your face
  • Anything wrinkled, stained, or carrying yesterday's smells
  • Hats and sunglasses indoors, headphones around your neck
  • Overpowering slogans, graphics, or novelty items — save your personality for your answers
  • Revealing or overly tight clothing in any professional setting; the interview should be remembered for your words

You do not need a new wardrobe or a large budget. Borrow a blazer, use a charity or second-hand shop for a quality suit, and spend your limited money on fit and a haircut rather than labels. What you wear will not get you the job — your preparation with our interview questions and your answer to "tell me about yourself" will do that. But the right outfit gets those answers a fair hearing, and that is exactly what it is for.

How to Follow Up After an Interview

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 9 min read

The interview ends, you go home — and then the waiting begins. What you do in that window matters more than most candidates realise. A prompt, well-written follow-up keeps you present in the hiring manager's mind, confirms your professionalism, and occasionally tips a close decision in your favour. Silence, by contrast, leaves your candidacy entirely in other people's hands. This guide covers the thank-you email, the follow-up when you hear nothing, and how to handle every outcome — including an offer and a rejection.

The thank-you email: send it within 24 hours

Send a short thank-you email to each person who interviewed you — or to the main interviewer with thanks passed to the panel — the same day or the following morning. Email is standard; a handwritten note is a memorable extra in traditional industries but should supplement, not replace, the email's speed. The message needs only four elements: thanks for their time, one specific thing from the conversation that increased your interest, one brief reminder connecting your experience to something they raised, and a courteous close. It should take five minutes to write and thirty seconds to read.

Subject: Thank you — interview for Marketing Assistant

Dear Ms. Garcia,

Thank you for speaking with me yesterday about the Marketing Assistant role. I particularly enjoyed hearing about the team's plans to expand its short-form video content — it's exactly the area where I've seen the strongest results in my current position, and our conversation left me even more enthusiastic about the role.

Please let me know if there's anything further I can provide. I look forward to hearing from you.

Best regards,
Amelia Hart

Personalise the specific detail for each interviewer. A generic thank-you copied to a whole panel reads as exactly that, and an email mentioning something only that person discussed quietly proves you listened — the same skill our professional email guide builds.

If you forgot something important

Realised in the car park that you never mentioned your most relevant project? The thank-you email can carry one — and only one — short addition: "I realised afterwards that I didn't mention my experience with X, which may be relevant given the team's plans for Y." One sentence, framed as helpful information rather than panic. Do not send a second email re-arguing your whole candidacy; it reads as insecurity, not enthusiasm.

When you hear nothing: the polite follow-up

First, respect the timeline you were given. If they said "we'll decide by Friday," do not chase on Thursday. If the date passes without news, wait two or three working days, then send one brief, friendly follow-up:

Subject: Following up — Marketing Assistant interview

Dear Ms. Garcia,

I hope you're well. I wanted to check whether there's any update on the Marketing Assistant position following my interview on the 12th. I remain very enthusiastic about the role and the team.

Thank you again for your time and consideration.

Best regards,
Amelia Hart

If that receives no reply, one further follow-up a week or so later is acceptable — then stop, and continue your search in parallel. Hiring delays are usually about budgets, calendars, and internal approvals, not about you; but a candidate who chases weekly quickly spends the goodwill the interview built. Never follow up by phone unless the employer invited calls, and never contact interviewers through personal social media.

While you wait: keep moving

The healthiest follow-up strategy includes your own behaviour. Write down everything you remember from the interview — the questions, your answers, the details about the role — while it is fresh; this record is gold if you reach a second round. Continue applying elsewhere and preparing with our interview questions guide. Momentum protects your confidence, and it also means a rejection, if it comes, lands on a moving target rather than your only hope.

Handling the outcomes

If you receive an offer

Thank them warmly, ask for the offer in writing, and take the agreed time to consider it — this is the starting gun for the approach in our salary negotiation guide. Do not resign from your current job until the new contract is confirmed.

If you receive a rejection

Reply graciously within a day: thank them for the opportunity, express genuine disappointment briefly, and — importantly — ask for feedback. "If you have a moment, I'd value any feedback on where my application fell short, as I'm keen to keep developing." Some employers will not give it, but many will, and a thoughtful reply keeps you first in mind when the successful candidate declines or a similar role opens — which happens far more often than candidates believe. Then use the feedback, adjust, and continue.

If you are kept as a reserve

Sometimes the answer is "you were a close second." Respond with warmth, confirm your continued interest explicitly, and check in once after a few weeks if a natural reason arises. Reserve candidates get hired regularly when first choices fall through — but only the ones the panel remembers fondly.

Following up well is a small set of habits: thank promptly and specifically, chase once politely and then stop, and respond to every outcome like a professional people would want on their team. The interview may be over, but your candidacy is not — manage its final stage as carefully as its first.

How to Switch Careers at 30 or 40

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 12 min read

Somewhere around thirty or forty, many people have the same quiet thought: "I can't do this for another twenty-five years — but surely it's too late to start again?" It is not too late, and you are not starting again. A career change at this stage is a translation exercise, not a reset: you carry a decade or two of skills, judgement, professional behaviour, and contacts into a new field, and the people who succeed are the ones who learn to present that experience in the new field's language. This guide gives you a realistic, staged plan — the same plan whether you are leaving teaching for tech, retail for healthcare, or an office for a trade.

Step 1: Get clear on what you are moving towards, and why

"Anything but this" is a feeling, not a direction, and changing careers on a feeling alone usually means landing in the same dissatisfaction with different wallpaper. Spend real time on two questions. First, what specifically are you leaving — the work itself, the pay ceiling, the hours, the management, the lack of growth? If the problem is your employer rather than your field, a new job may fix it at a tenth of the cost of a career change. Second, what are you moving towards? Shortlist two or three target fields and research them properly: day-to-day reality, entry routes, realistic pay at entry and at five years, demand in your area, and the qualifications that genuinely gate entry. Talk to people doing the job — a twenty-minute conversation with a practitioner is worth a week of reading, and most people are flattered to be asked.

Step 2: Audit your transferable skills

List everything your current career has actually trained you in, ignoring job titles: managing people or budgets, training others, handling difficult customers, analysing data, meeting deadlines under pressure, selling, writing, organising complex schedules, resolving conflicts, using specific software. Then look at your target field's job adverts and mark the overlaps. You will usually find that 50–70% of what the new field wants, you already do under different names. A teacher moving into corporate training brings presentation, curriculum design, assessment, and patience with difficult rooms. A retail manager moving into operations brings team leadership, stock systems, targets, and customer data. This audit becomes the backbone of your new resume — and your confidence.

Step 3: Close the real gaps — only the real ones

Every field has a short list of genuinely required credentials and a longer list of things that merely look nice. Identify the gates: the licence, certificate, or qualification without which you cannot legally or practically be hired. Then find the fastest credible route to them — part-time and online study while you keep earning is the pattern that works for most adults with bills. Alongside formal credentials, build proof: a portfolio, a project, volunteering in the new field, freelance pieces. Employers hiring career changers look for demonstrated commitment; six months of evening study and a finished project answers their biggest doubt — "is this person serious, or just restless?" — better than any interview speech.

Step 4: Test the water before you leap

Reduce the risk by sampling the new field first: shadow someone for a day, volunteer a few hours a week, take one freelance project, enrol in the first module before the full course. Real contact with the work either confirms the direction — energising the harder steps ahead — or saves you from an expensive mistake. It also starts your network in the new field, and networks, as every guide on this site repeats, are how most jobs actually happen. Update your LinkedIn profile gradually as your direction firms up: follow the new field's voices, join its groups, and let your headline evolve when you are ready to be found for it.

Step 5: Rewrite your story, don't apologise for it

Your application materials must present the change as a deliberate, positive move. In your cover letter, spend two or three sentences on the why — framed forward ("After ten years in hospitality, I'm bringing my customer operations experience into facilities management, where…") — then move immediately to your transferable evidence and your new credentials. In interviews, expect the question and answer it with the structure from our guide on "tell me about yourself": present competence, past experience translated into the new language, and a future pointed firmly at this field. Never frame yourself as escaping a failed career. You are a professional making a considered move, carrying valuable experience with you. Interviewers take their cue from your framing.

Step 6: Plan the money honestly

Most career changes involve a temporary step down — in seniority, in pay, or both — before the climb resumes, usually faster than a beginner's because your professional maturity shows. Plan for it: build whatever savings buffer you can before resigning, calculate your true minimum income, and consider bridge options such as part-time work in the old field while training for the new one. A change made from financial panic rarely survives its first hard month; a change with six months of runway usually does. If a pay negotiation arises at the entry point of the new field, your experience still counts — negotiate using the method in our salary guide, anchored to the value of your maturity and transferable skills, not only your years in the field.

The mindset that makes it work

You will be a beginner again, alongside people fifteen years younger, and some days that will sting. Remember what you actually are: a beginner with a professional's habits — reliability, judgement, communication, and a work ethic already proven. Those are the qualities employers struggle most to find, and they are why experienced changers typically rise faster than true beginners once through the door. At thirty you likely have thirty-five working years ahead; at forty, twenty-five. Spending two of them repositioning into work you can sustain and grow in is not a late start. It is one of the best investments available to you. Begin with the audit this week — your future field is closer than it looks from here.

How to Build a Personal Brand at Work

By the Career Boost Team · Updated November 2026 · 10 min read

You already have a personal brand at work, whether you have thought about it or not. It is the sentence colleagues use when your name comes up: "She's the one who calms down angry clients." "He's brilliant with spreadsheets but never answers email." "If you need it organised, ask her." That sentence decides which projects you are offered, whose names are mentioned in promotion discussions, and who gets called when an opportunity appears. Building a personal brand simply means taking deliberate control of that sentence — making sure it is accurate, positive, and known by the people whose opinions shape your career.

Step 1: Decide what you want to be known for

A strong professional brand rests on two or three qualities, not ten. Choose them at the intersection of three things: what you are genuinely good at, what your organisation values, and what you enjoy enough to do consistently for years. Reliable finisher. Clear communicator. The person who turns messy data into decisions. The calm head in a crisis. Write your chosen combination down as one sentence — "I want to be known as the person who makes complex projects feel organised and delivers them early" — because every action in this guide is about making that sentence true in other people's minds. Authenticity is not a garnish here: a brand built on qualities you do not have collapses at the first real test, usually publicly.

Step 2: Do the work that proves it — visibly

Reputation is built from evidence, and evidence needs an audience. This does not mean self-promotion in the crude sense; it means making sure good work is seen by the right people as a natural part of how you operate. Send the brief completion update when a project lands, with the result stated plainly. Present your team's work in meetings when volunteers are requested. Write the summary document others forward. Share credit generously and specifically — naming colleagues' contributions in front of others builds your reputation as a leader faster than claiming sole credit ever will, and it is also simply true. The principle: let people discover your competence through your work's visibility, not through your announcements about it.

Step 3: Be consistent in the small things

Brands are built less by big moments than by a hundred small, repeated signals. Reply when you said you would reply. Arrive prepared. Keep your written communication clear and courteous — your emails are a daily broadcast of your brand, which is why our guide on professional email matters beyond the inbox. Meet deadlines, or renegotiate them early when reality changes. Consistency is what turns "she did a great job on that project" into "she's the reliable one" — the second sentence is a brand; the first is just an event. Conversely, one visible pattern of lateness, gossip, or blame can overwrite months of good signals, so guard the basics relentlessly.

Step 4: Build your network inside the building

Your brand only exists in rooms you are not in if people in those rooms know you. Invest deliberately in relationships beyond your immediate team: help colleagues in other departments, join cross-functional projects, attend the optional talks, remember names and follow up on conversations. Be useful without keeping score — the person who connects two colleagues, shares a useful contact, or explains a process patiently becomes known across the organisation as a resource, and resources get recommended. These relationships are also your early-warning system for opportunities and your support structure when you later ask for a promotion or navigate a difficult manager.

Step 5: Let your online presence match

Your brand now extends beyond the building. When a manager, client, or recruiter searches your name — and they will — your LinkedIn profile should tell the same story your colleagues would: same strengths, same direction, evidenced the same way. Occasional, thoughtful online activity reinforces it: sharing a useful article with a line of your own insight, commenting intelligently on your field's discussions, posting a short reflection when a project teaches you something. Keep it professional and consistent; one careless public post can contradict a year of careful in-person brand building.

Step 6: Collect proof and keep it current

Maintain the same evidence file recommended in our promotion guide: results with numbers, positive feedback saved as it arrives, projects and responsibilities beyond your job description. Your brand is only as strong as your ability to evidence it in the moments that matter — reviews, promotion cases, raise requests, and eventually applications elsewhere. Review your one-sentence brand every six months: is it still what you want to be known for? Is the evidence growing? As your career develops, the sentence should evolve — from reliable pair of hands, to trusted specialist, to the person who develops others. That evolution, visible and documented, is a career compounding in public.

What personal branding is not

  • It is not bragging. Talking about yourself constantly repels the very people you need. Let work and results speak; your job is distribution, not volume.
  • It is not a costume. Performing an identity you cannot sustain — the always-available hero, the office comedian — exhausts you and eventually cracks.
  • It is not office politics. Undermining colleagues, hoarding information, or managing impressions while neglecting the work produces a brand too — the kind that ends careers when it matures.
  • It is not instant. Reputations form over months of consistent evidence. Anyone promising a shortcut is selling the costume version.

Start this week: write your one sentence, pick one piece of good work to make properly visible, and fix one small inconsistency between the brand you want and the signals you send. Repeat for a year, and the sentence people use about you will be the one you chose.

About Career Boost

Career Boost is a career-advice website built on a simple observation: most people are never taught how hiring and promotion actually work. They are taught their subjects, their trades, and their professions — and then left to guess at resumes, interviews, negotiation, and office politics, usually learning by expensive trial and error. We publish practical, step-by-step guides that close that gap.

What we publish

Every guide on Career Boost is written to be used, not just read. That means concrete steps in a sensible order, example sentences and complete templates you can adapt, honest explanations of what employers are really looking for, and clear warnings about the mistakes that quietly cost people opportunities. Our library covers the full arc of a working life: writing your first CV with no experience, preparing for interviews, communicating well at work, negotiating salary, earning promotion, changing direction at 30 or 40, and leaving a job gracefully when the time comes.

How we write

All content on this site is original, written for Career Boost, and written in plain English. We do not copy material from other websites, and we do not pad articles with filler — if a guide is long, it is because the topic deserves the space. We aim for advice that stays true across industries and countries: the specifics of labour law vary, but a clear resume, a structured interview answer, and a professional email work everywhere. Where numbers or customs differ by location, our guides say so and tell you how to find your local answer.

Who this site is for

Students and graduates looking for a first foothold. Experienced professionals who have been passed over and want to understand why. People returning to work after a break, changing careers, or preparing for a conversation about pay that they have been postponing for years. If you have ever thought "I know I can do the job — I just don't know how to get the chance to show it," this site was written for you.

Our promise

No hype, no miracle claims, and no advice we would not give a friend. Career progress is usually the compound interest of small, well-executed steps: a resume rewritten properly, one interview prepared thoroughly, one email sent at the right moment. Our job is to make each of those steps as clear as we can. Your job — and we know it is the harder one — is to take them. Start with the guide that matches the problem in front of you today, on our guides page.

If you have a question, a correction, or a topic you would like us to cover, we would genuinely like to hear it — see our contact page.

Frequently Asked Questions

Straight answers to the career questions we are asked most often. For anything not covered here, you will usually find a full guide in our guides library.

How long should my resume be?

One page if you have less than ten years of experience; two pages for experienced professionals whose history genuinely needs the space. Length is not the goal — relevance is. Every line should support your application for this specific job. See how to write a resume that gets interviews.

Should I include a cover letter if it is marked optional?

Yes, in almost every case. An "optional" cover letter is a free opportunity to explain your fit in your own words, and few applicants take it — which is exactly why it helps you stand out. Keep it under one page and tailor it to the employer. See how to write a cover letter that stands out.

Can I really get hired with no experience?

Yes. Employers hire beginners constantly, especially in retail, hospitality, customer service, care, logistics, and administration. What they need is evidence of ability and reliability — coursework, volunteering, projects, and part-time work all provide it when presented well. See how to find a job with no experience and how to write a CV with no experience.

How do I explain a gap in my employment history?

Briefly, honestly, and without apology: one sentence stating the reason, anything productive from the period, and then your readiness for work now. Never falsify dates. Most employers have seen every kind of gap and care far more about the explanation being straightforward. See how to explain a gap in your CV.

What should I wear to an interview at a casual company?

Dress one level smarter than the company's everyday standard. For a casual workplace, that usually means smart trousers or dark neat jeans, a proper shirt or blouse, and a blazer — clean, pressed, and comfortable. When in doubt, err on the formal side. See what to wear to a job interview.

When should I bring up salary?

As late as you reasonably can — ideally after the employer has decided they want you, because that is when your negotiating position is strongest. Research your market range from the start so you are never caught unprepared, but let the employer name the first number where possible. See how to negotiate your salary with confidence.

Is it acceptable to ask for a raise by email?

Yes — particularly with remote managers or formal review processes. The strongest raise emails present quantified evidence, anchor the request in market research, name a specific figure, and close by requesting a meeting to discuss it. See how to ask for a raise by email for complete templates.

How long should I wait before following up after an interview?

Send a thank-you email within 24 hours. If the employer's stated decision date passes without news, wait two or three working days, then send one short, polite follow-up. One more a week later is the limit. See how to follow up after an interview.

I am 40. Is it too late to change careers?

No. You likely have twenty-five working years ahead — more than enough for a full second career. The key is translating your existing experience into the new field's language, closing only the credential gaps that genuinely gate entry, and planning the financial transition honestly. See how to switch careers at 30 or 40.

How much notice do I have to give when I resign?

Your contract controls this — check it before you say anything. Common notice periods range from one week to three months depending on the role and country. Whatever the period, tell your manager in person first, then confirm with a short, professional letter the same day. See how to write a resignation letter for examples.

My boss is making my job miserable. What should I do first?

Start by defining the specific behaviours, not the person, and try the practical strategies for your situation — proactive updates for micromanagers, written confirmations for unclear bosses, visibility habits against credit-taking. Document significant incidents factually, have one calm conversation focused on behaviour and solutions, and use formal channels if the behaviour crosses into bullying or discrimination. See how to handle a difficult boss professionally.

Does Career Boost offer personal coaching or resume writing services?

No. Career Boost is a free advice website; we do not offer paid coaching, resume writing, or placement services, and we never charge readers for our guides. Everything we publish is available on this site for anyone to read and use.

Privacy Policy

Last updated: November 2026

This Privacy Policy explains what information is collected when you visit Career Boost (careerboosthub.github.io), how it is used, and the choices you have. We have written it in plain language, and we keep it simple because our practices are simple: this is a content website that you can read without creating an account or submitting personal information.

Information we collect

Information you give us. The only personal information we receive directly is what you choose to send us by email — typically your email address, your name if you sign your message, and the contents of your message. We use it solely to read and reply to your enquiry.

Automatically collected information. Like most websites, basic technical information may be processed by our hosting provider and, where enabled, analytics and advertising partners. This can include your IP address, browser type, device information, the pages you visit, and the time of your visit. This information is aggregated and statistical; we do not use it to identify individual readers.

Cookies

Cookies are small files stored on your device by your browser. This site itself is a static website and does not set its own account or login cookies. However, third-party services used on this site — such as Google Analytics and Google AdSense or other advertising partners — may set cookies to measure traffic, understand how readers use the site, and display advertising. Advertising cookies may be used to show ads based on your previous visits to this and other websites. You can control or delete cookies at any time through your browser settings, and you can opt out of personalised advertising through Google's Ads Settings. Disabling cookies will not prevent you from reading any content on this site.

Advertising

Career Boost may display advertising provided by Google AdSense and other third-party advertising partners. These partners may use cookies and similar technologies to serve ads based on your interests and browsing activity, and to measure the performance of those ads. We do not control the cookies set by third-party advertisers; their use is governed by their own privacy policies. We do not sell personal information to anyone.

Analytics

We may use Google Analytics or a similar service to understand which guides readers find useful, so we can improve the site. Analytics data is processed in aggregate form — for example, how many people read a particular guide — and is not used to build profiles of individual visitors by name.

How we use information

  • To operate, maintain, and improve this website and its content
  • To respond to emails you send us
  • To understand readership in aggregate and decide what to publish next
  • To display advertising that keeps the site free to read
  • To comply with legal obligations where they apply

Sharing of information

We do not sell, rent, or trade your personal information. Information may be processed by the service providers described above (hosting, analytics, and advertising) strictly in order to provide those services, and may be disclosed if required by law.

External links

Our guides may link to external websites for further reading. We are not responsible for the privacy practices or content of external sites, and we encourage you to read their policies.

Children's privacy

Career Boost is written for adults and students preparing for work. It is not directed at children under 13, and we do not knowingly collect personal information from them.

Your choices

You may browse this site without providing any personal information. You may block cookies in your browser, use your browser's private mode, and opt out of personalised advertising through your Google account settings. If you have emailed us and would like your message deleted, contact us at the address below and we will do so.

Changes to this policy

We may update this policy from time to time. The date at the top of this page shows when it was last revised, and continued use of the site after changes are posted constitutes acceptance of the updated policy.

Contact
